content: Gum disease, also known as gingivitis, refers to the inflammation of the gums (gingiva). It is a condition that can lead to more severe periodontal diseases if left untreated. Symptoms of Gum Disease: Gums that bleed easily, such as when brushing teeth gently, may indicate gum disease. The gums may appear bright red or have a red-purple discoloration. Tenderness in the gums when touched, although they are typically painless otherwise. The presence of mouth sores. Swelling of the gums. A shiny appearance of the gums. Causes of Gum Disease: Gingivitis is a type of periodontal disease, which involves inflammation and infection that can damage the tissues supporting the teeth, including the gums, periodontal ligaments, and the tooth sockets (alveolar bone). The primary cause of gingivitis is the long-term accumulation of plaque, a sticky substance composed of bacteria, mucus, and food debris that forms on the exposed surfaces of teeth. If plaque is not removed, it hardens into tartar, which becomes trapped at the base of the teeth. Both plaque and tartar irritate and inflame the gums. Bacteria and their toxins further contribute to gum infection, swelling, and tenderness. Injury to the gums, such as from overly aggressive brushing or flossing, can also lead to gingivitis. Several factors increase the risk of developing gingivitis, including: General illnesses. Poor dental hygiene. Hormonal changes during pregnancy, which make the gums more sensitive. Uncontrolled diabetes. Misaligned teeth, rough edges on dental fillings, and poorly fitting or unclean dental appliances (e.g., braces, dentures, bridges, crowns) that irritate the gums. Certain medications, such as phenytoin and birth control pills, as well as exposure to heavy metals like lead and bismuth. High-Risk Groups: Gingivitis is common and can affect individuals to varying degrees. It often develops during puberty or early adulthood due to hormonal changes and may persist or recur depending on the health of the teeth and gums. Diagnosis: A dentist will examine the mouth and teeth, looking for soft, swollen, red-purple gums. Plaque and tartar deposits may be visible at the base of the teeth. The gums are usually painless or only mildly tender. Additional tests, such as dental X-rays or measurements of dental bone levels, may be performed to assess whether the inflammation has spread to the supporting structures of the teeth. When to Seek Medical Care: Contact your dentist if you notice symptoms of gingivitis, especially if you have not had a routine cleaning and examination in the past six months. If your dentist identifies underlying conditions contributing to gingivitis, they may recommend medical treatment from a healthcare provider. Treatment Options: The primary goal of treatment is to reduce inflammation. A dentist or dental hygienist will thoroughly clean the teeth, using various instruments or devices to remove plaque and tartar deposits. After professional cleaning, maintaining meticulous oral hygiene is essential. The dentist or hygienist will provide instructions on proper brushing and flossing techniques. For severe cases, professional cleaning may be recommended twice a year or more frequently. Antibacterial mouth rinses or other aids may be suggested in addition to regular brushing and flossing. In some cases, correcting misaligned teeth or replacing dental appliances may be necessary. Any related illnesses or conditions should also be addressed. Prognosis: Removing plaque from inflamed gums can be uncomfortable, but symptoms such as bleeding and tenderness should improve within one to two weeks after professional cleaning and consistent oral hygiene. Warm saltwater rinses or antibacterial mouth rinses can help reduce gum swelling. Over-the-counter anti-inflammatory medications can alleviate discomfort following a thorough cleaning. Healthy gums are pink and firm in appearance. Lifelong strict oral hygiene is necessary to prevent the recurrence of gingivitis. Possible Complications: Recurrence of gingivitis. Progression to periodontitis. Infection or abscess formation in the gums or jawbones. Development of trench mouth (a severe form of gum infection). Prevention: Good oral hygiene is the most effective way to prevent gingivitis, as it removes the plaque responsible for the condition. Brush your teeth at least twice daily and floss gently at least once a day. For individuals prone to gingivitis, brushing and flossing after every meal and before bedtime may be recommended. Consult your dentist or dental hygienist for guidance on proper brushing and flossing techniques. Special tools or appliances, such as specific types of toothbrushes, toothpicks, or water irrigation devices, may be recommended for individuals particularly susceptible to plaque buildup. Antiplaque or antitartar toothpaste and mouth rinses may also be suggested. Regular professional tooth cleaning is crucial to remove plaque that may develop despite careful brushing and flossing. Many dentists recommend professional cleaning at least every six months.
